answer.rationale:
memory_c2 is the single load-bearing memory for the switch option, because the low-cost vendor's quote is the only path that hits the 18% mandate on its own. But as written it only attests to unit cost, onboarding speed, and invoicing accuracy — it is silent on on-time delivery, quality escapes, ramp volume, and whether the part it covered was as constrained as this one. Those omissions are exactly the dimensions that matter when the line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer and the contract lapses in 14 days. So I spend the one verification pull there rather than on the incumbent memories, which are mutually corroborating (c1 continuity, c4 renegotiation leverage, c6 volume pricing) and point the same direction anyway.

Absent verification, a primary-vendor switch executed inside a 14-day window against a zero-buffer line converts a cost problem into a delivery-outage problem, which violates the stated constraint of not increasing delivery risk. I therefore intend to negotiate terms with the incumbent, using the low-cost quote as the explicit benchmark — c4 shows benchmarking has actually moved this incumbent on price and payment terms, and c6 shows term length is a lever that cut cost without narrowing service scope. I keep this a small guarded step: a short bridge or single-cycle term rather than a multi-year lock, so the next review retains the option to switch or dual-source once the low-cost vendor is qualified at volume (c3's second-source pattern is the natural follow-on, but it is not this cycle's one decision).

Risk I am flagging: an 18% mandate applied through price alone tends to be absorbed downstream as reduced expediting, thinner allocation priority, or looser quality tolerance — cost moves on paper while risk migrates somewhere unmeasured. Negotiation should hold service scope and delivery commitments explicit, not just headline price. Residual uncertainty stands: if the archive shows c2's switch actually held OTD through a comparable constrained ramp, switching becomes materially more defensible and I would revise toward it, possibly still staged rather than wholesale. If c2 turns out to cover a non-critical, low-volume, unconstrained part, its apparent support for switching largely evaporates.
